Linear Transformation. A function between two vector spaces that preserves the vector space structure.

Formally, a linear transformation T from V to W satisfies the property that T applied to any scalar multiple of a sum of vectors equals that scalar multiple applied to the sum of the transformed vectors. Linear transformations are the natural maps in algebra, encoding rotations, reflections, scalings, and projections in a unified framework. Every linear transformation between finite-dimensional spaces can be represented by a matrix, connecting abstract algebra to practical computation.

A linear transformation must satisfy additivity: the transformation of a sum equals the sum of the transformations. It must also satisfy homogeneity: the transformation of a scalar times a vector equals that scalar times the transformation of the vector. Every linear transformation from n-dimensional to m-dimensional real space corresponds uniquely to an m by n matrix. Given a column vector, the transformation equals the matrix times that vector.

The kernel of a transformation is the set of vectors mapping to zero. The image is the set of all output vectors. The rank-nullity theorem states that the dimension of the kernel plus the dimension of the image equals the dimension of the domain. This fundamental constraint relates these two dimensions. A transformation is injective, or one-to-one, if only zero maps to zero. It is surjective, or onto, if every target vector is reached. It is bijective, or invertible, if both.

Eigenvalues and eigenvectors describe the transformation's directions of pure scaling. Along these directions, the transformation merely multiplies by a scalar. The trace and determinant of the matrix representation encode global properties: the trace equals the sum of eigenvalues, the determinant equals their product. Linear transformations permeate science: rotations in computer graphics, diffusion in partial differential equations, quantum mechanics operators, and machine learning embeddings. Different bases give different matrices for the same transformation, but similarity transformations relate them.
